Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Use the complex inner product convention linear in its first argument. Give the exterior algebra its induced inner product, with an orthonormal wedge basis. Exterior multiplication is e(v)η=v∧η. Its adjoint is contraction:
e(b)∗(v1​∧⋯∧vr​)=∑j=1r​(−1)j−1(vj​,b)v1​∧⋯vj​⋯∧vr​.
(1)
Applying this formula to a∧η separates its first term from the remaining terms, giving e(b)∗e(a)η=(a,b)η−e(a)e(b)∗η. Hence the canonical anticommutation relations are
e(a)e(b)∗+e(b)∗e(a)=(a,b)I.​
(2)
For irreducibility, choose an orthonormal basis u1​,…,ud​. The occupancy projections are Nj​=e(uj​)e(uj​)∗, and P0​=∏j​(I−Nj​) projects onto the vacuum 1∈Λ0V. For an increasing index set J, put EJ​=e(uj1​​)⋯e(ujr​​). Then EI​P0​EJ∗​ maps the wedge basis vector uJ​ to uI​ and kills every other wedge basis vector. Thus these products are all matrix units and the generated star-algebra is End(ΛV). Any common invariant subspace for the creation and annihilation operators is therefore either zero or all of W.

b OurBigBook.com
The commutant is A′={T∈EndV:Ta=aT for every a∈A}. Clearly A⊆A′′. For the reverse inclusion, first note that Aξ is an invariant subspace for the unital star-algebra A, and its orthogonal complement is invariant too. Its projection belongs to A′. Thus if B∈A′′, Bξ∈Aξ.
To make the same algebra element work for all vectors, amplify to Vd, where d=dimV. The diagonal action a(d) has commutant consisting of block matrices whose entries belong to A′. Therefore B(d) commutes with this amplified commutant. For a basis ξ1​,…,ξd​, the subspace {(aξ1​,…,aξd​):a∈A} is invariant and reducing for the amplified algebra. Its projection lies in that commutant. The preceding argument gives some a∈A with (Bξ1​,…,Bξd​)=(aξ1​,…,aξd​). Since these vectors form a basis, B=a. Hence
A′′=A.​
(3)
This finite-dimensional double commutant theorem for star-algebras uses the star hypothesis to make the orbit subspaces reducing.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
A strongly continuous unitary representation of the circle group decomposes as H=⨁​m∈Z​Hm​, with Uz​ξ=zmξ on Hm​. Its positive energy unitary representation of the circle condition is that the occurring integers are bounded below. Equivalently Ueit​=eitL with a self-adjoint generator bounded below. An integer character can shift the lowest weight to zero.
Let M=S′′. Because S=S∗, this is a Von Neumann algebra, and rotation invariance makes Uz​M′Uz∗​=M′. Joint irreducibility implies M′∩{Uz​}′=CI: a nonscalar self-adjoint element of that joint commutant would have a nontrivial invariant spectral projection gives a reducing subspace.
For T∈M′, take its strong Fourier coefficients Tk​=∫T​z−kUz​TUz∗​dz. They lie in M′ and satisfy Uz​Tk​Uz∗​=zkTk​. Both Tk∗​Tk​ and Tk​Tk∗​ are rotation-invariant elements of M′, hence scalar. If Tk​=0, both scalars equal ∥Tk​∥2, so Tk​/∥Tk​∥ is a unitary. It shifts energy by k. For k=0, applying it or its adjoint to a nonzero lowest-energy vector produces a vector below the lowest energy, a contradiction. Thus Tk​=0 for every k=0, while T0​ is scalar.
Fejér sum averaging of the strongly continuous orbit Uz​TUz∗​ converges strongly to T. Its Fourier coefficients have just shown every such average is T0​, so T=T0​ is scalar. In particular every bounded operator commuting with S commutes with every Uz​. In fact the hypotheses force the stronger conclusion S′=CI.

a OurBigBook.com
Write X=I+E. Use a submultiplicative Sobolev algebra norm for which the Fourier projections are contractive, and its compatible matrix/column norms. The numeric hypothesis ∥E∥<1 is understood in this algebra norm; the unscaled Fourier Sobolev norm need not have multiplication constant one.
Let A>0​ and A<0​ denote the strictly positive and strictly negative Fourier subspaces. The equation y+​=−P>0​(E+Ey+​) is a contraction on Mn​(A>0​), so it has a unique solution. Put Y+​=I+y+​ and Z−​=XY+​. The equation says Z−​∈Mn​(A−​), and Y+​(0)=I. Similarly the contraction v−​=−P<0​(E+v−​E) gives V−​=I+v−​ with Z+​=V−​X∈Mn​(A+​). No invertibility of these solutions has yet been assumed.
Now V−​Z−​=Z+​Y+​ belongs to both Fourier subalgebras, hence is a constant matrix C. Taking constant coefficients on either side shows C=Z−​(0)=Z+​(0). We claim C is invertible. If Cv=0, then the Hardy compression TX​=P≥0​X annihilates Y+​v, because P≥0​Z−​v=Cv=0. But TX​=I+P≥0​E on the Hardy Sobolev space has inverse given by a Neumann series, since the perturbation has norm less than one. Thus Y+​v=0, and its constant coefficient is v, forcing v=0. Finite-dimensionality proves the claim.
Consequently C−1Z+​ is a left inverse of Y+​, and C−1V−​ is a left inverse of Z−​. Matrix entries are functions in a commutative algebra, so pointwise finite-dimensional inversion makes these left inverses two-sided inverses in their respective Fourier subalgebras. Set
X−​=Z−​,X+​=Y+−1​.​
(4)
Then X=X−​X+​, both factors are invertible in the stated algebras, and X+​(0)=I. If two normalized factorizations exist, X−−1​X−​=X+​X+−1​ lies in A−​∩A+​ and is constant; evaluating the analytic side at zero makes it I. This proves uniqueness. The argument is near-identity Sobolev loop factorization and, crucially, proves invertibility rather than treating the contraction solution itself as automatically invertible.

Give G(H) its natural trace-class topology: differentiability means F(t+h)=F(t)+hF˙(t)+o1​(h), with remainder small in trace norm. The Fredholm determinant is the continuous extension of finite-rank determinants; it is multiplicative by finite-rank approximation and satisfies
det(I+K)=1+TrK+O(∥K∥12​)
(5)
near zero. For example its exterior-power series bounds the remainder by e∥K∥1​−1−∥K∥1​, proving that estimate directly.
Factor F(t+h)=F(t)[I+hF(t)−1F˙(t)+o1​(h)]. Multiplicativity and the preceding expansion give
dtd​detF(t)=detF(t)Tr(F(t)−1F˙(t)).​
(6)
The determinant is nonzero for invertible F, so division yields the required logarithmic derivative. Differentiability only in the bounded-operator norm would not justify this trace formula; the specified topology is essential.

Let C=[A,B] be trace class and set F(t)=etAeBe−tAe−B. The integral identity eBAe−B−A=∫01​esB[B,A]e−sBds is trace-norm convergent. It shows that this difference is trace class. The analogous Duhamel identity then makes F(t)−I trace class and differentiable in that norm. Hence F(t)∈G(H).
Compute the right logarithmic derivative without taking separate traces of A:
F˙F−1=etA(A−eBAe−B)e−tA.
(7)
Trace invariance under bounded invertible similarity and the integral identity give Tr(F˙F−1)=−∫01​Tr[B,A]ds=Tr[A,B]. Cyclicity with a trace-class factor makes this equal to the trace in part (b). As F(0)=I, integrating the scalar differential equation gives
det(eAeBe−Ae−B)=expTr[A,B].​
(8)
This Fredholm determinant of an exponential commutator can be nontrivial in infinite dimension: it is not legitimate to set the trace of a trace-class commutator to zero when A,B themselves need not be trace class.

Split f=f−​+a0​+f+​ into strictly negative and strictly positive Fourier parts, and let A=T(f−​), B=T(f+​). The Toeplitz multiplication rule is T(g)T(h)=T(gh) when g is coanalytic or h is analytic. It follows directly because the discarded negative Fourier part cannot return to the Hardy space in those cases. Thus exponentiation within either subalgebra is exact, and
T(ef)T(e−f)=eAeBe−Ae−B.
(9)
The constant terms cancel. If S=T(z) is the unilateral shift, A=∑m>0​a−m​(S∗)m and B=∑n>0​an​Sn. The commutator [(S∗)m,Sn] is finite rank, with trace n when m=n and zero otherwise. For equal powers it is the projection onto the first n basis vectors; for unequal powers its matrix has no diagonal entries. Its trace norm is bounded by 2min(m,n). Smoothness of f makes the weighted double coefficient sum finite, so the commutator series converges in trace norm and
Tr[A,B]=∑n>0​nan​a−n​.
(10)
Applying part (c) proves the Toeplitz exponential determinant identity
det(T(ef)T(e−f))=exp(n>0∑​nan​a−n​).​
(11)
In particular the product is an invertible identity-plus-trace-class operator, so the determinant in the formula is well-defined.

a OurBigBook.com
A unitary family with the required Weyl relations is
(W(x,y)f)(t)=eixy+2iytf(t+x).​
(12)
Translations preserve the L2 norm and the multiplier has modulus one. Multiplication of two such operators leaves the phase x1​y2​−y1​x2​ after extracting W(x1​+x2​,y1​+y2​), proving the relation. Translation and modulation are strongly continuous, first on compactly supported smooth functions by direct estimates, then on all of L2 by density and unitarity.
If a bounded operator A commutes with all W, it commutes with translations and every modulation e2iyt. The spectral theorem for the multiplication coordinate therefore makes it commute with all bounded multiplication operators and interval projections. One can see its form directly: on a finite interval I, set hI​=A1I​. For bounded ϕ supported in I, commutation gives Aϕ=ϕhI​. Testing characteristic functions shows ∣hI​∣≤∥A∥ almost everywhere. On increasing intervals these functions agree on overlaps and yield a single h∈L∞ with A=Mh​.
Commutation with translations says h(t+x)=h(t) almost everywhere for every x. Convolving with a smooth approximate identity produces smooth functions invariant under every translation, hence constants. Passing to the local L1 limit makes h constant almost everywhere. Therefore A is a scalar operator, and the unitary family acts irreducibly.

b OurBigBook.com
Let W be the given regular irreducible family. Write a=(x,y) and a∧b=x1​y2​−y1​x2​. Define the strongly integrated operator
P=π1​∫R2​e−∣a∣2/2W(a)da.
(13)
The Gaussian is integrable and the operators are unitary, so the integral defines a bounded operator on each vector. The Weyl relation and W(a)∗=W(−a) give P∗=P. For its square, the coefficient at W(c) is
π21​∫e−(∣a∣2+∣c−a∣2)/2eia∧cda=π1​e−∣c∣2/2,
(14)
by the two-dimensional Gaussian integral. Thus P2=P. The same Gaussian integration, with an inserted Weyl operator, gives
PW(b)P=e−∣b∣2/2P.​
(15)
This is the Gaussian projection in a Weyl representation.
It is nonzero. Otherwise all its conjugates would vanish; the Weyl relation makes their matrix coefficients the Fourier transforms of e−∣a∣2/2(W(a)ξ,η), with the dual variable 2b∧a. Uniqueness of the Fourier transform of an integrable function would make each such function zero. Strong continuity then makes its value at zero vanish, contradicting (ξ,ξ)>0 for a nonzero vector.
Choose a unit vector v∈PH. Irreducibility makes the span of W(a)v dense. If w∈PH is perpendicular to v, the boxed identity makes it perpendicular to this entire span, so w=0. Hence P has rank one, and its identity gives (W(a)v,v)=e−∣a∣2/2.
In the concrete representation of part (a), the Gaussian v0​(t)=(2/π)1/4e−t2 has precisely this expectation. With the linear-in-first inner-product convention, both orbit families have Gram matrix
(W(a)v,W(b)v)=eia∧be−∣a−b∣2/2=(W(a)v0​,W(b)v0​).
(16)
Therefore the map ∑cj​W(aj​)v0​↦∑cj​W(aj​)v is well-defined and isometric. Its source and target spans are dense, so it extends to a unitary operator intertwiner. This proves the unitary equivalence, the Stone-von Neumann theorem in the normalization of this question, rather than invoking that theorem as the proof.

The real matrix g=(ac​bd​) with determinant one preserves u∧v. Hence Wg​(u)=W(gu) obeys the same Weyl relations. It is strongly continuous and irreducible because g is invertible and its arguments range over the whole plane. Part (b) gives a unitary V intertwining W and Wg​, so VW(u)V∗=W(gu). If V1​,V2​ both work, V2∗​V1​ commutes with all W and is scalar by part (a); its scalar has modulus one. Thus the implementer is unique up to phase.
For the displayed quarter-turn, choose the scaled inverse Fourier transform
(Vf)(s)=π−1/2∫R​e2istf(t)dt.​
(17)
The formula starts on Schwartz functions and extends unitarily to L2 by Plancherel and a change of scale. It conjugates Tx​f(t)=f(t+x) to multiplication by e−2ixs, and multiplication by e2iyt to Ty​. Keeping the Weyl phase therefore gives VW(x,y)V∗=W(y,−x), as required. With the opposite Fourier-kernel sign one obtains the opposite quarter-turn, so that convention must be checked.

One form of the Jacobi triple product is, for 0<∣q∣<1 and z=0,
n∈Z∑​qn2zn=j=1∏∞​(1−q2j)(1+zq2j−1)(1+z−1q2j−1).​
(18)
Both sides converge locally uniformly on the punctured z plane. Here is a finite-product proof which also determines the multiplicative constant.
Put Q=q2 and (Q;Q)m​=∏j=1m​(1−Qj), with value one at m=0. Define the Gaussian binomial coefficient [km​]Q​=(Q;Q)m​/[(Q;Q)k​(Q;Q)m−k​]. The recurrence [km​]Q​=[km−1​]Q​+Qm−k[k−1m−1​]Q​ proves by induction that
∏j=0m−1​(1+tQj)=∑k=0m​Qk(k−1)/2[km​]Q​tk.
(19)
Rewrite the two finite factors as
∏j=1N​(1+zq2j−1)(1+z−1q2j−1)=z−NqN2∏j=02N−1​(1+zq1−2NQj).
(20)
The finite identity, with n=k−N, makes this ∑n=−NN​znqn2[N+n2N​]Q​. Multiply by (Q;Q)N​. For each fixed integer n, the resulting coefficient tends to one, because (Q;Q)m​ tends to a nonzero limit and [N+n2N​]Q​→1/(Q;Q)∞​.
All finite (Q;Q)m​ are uniformly bounded above and away from zero. Thus these coefficients have one uniform bound, and ∑n∈Z​∣q∣n2∣z∣n is uniformly summable on compact annuli. Dominated convergence passes the limit through the finite sums and proves the boxed formula. At q=0 the formula follows by its limiting value one. The frequently used alternative form is
∏j≥1​(1−tj)(1+utj−1)(1+u−1tj)=∑m∈Z​umtm(m−1)/2,∣t∣<1.
(21)
It follows by the substitution q2=t, z=u/q, and is the version used for the charge-counting identity in Question 8.

b OurBigBook.com
Write p:U(H)→PU(H) for the scalar quotient. Local strongly continuous sections exist: near a fixed projective unitary, fix its phase by requiring one nonzero matrix coefficient, taken relative to a fixed representative, to be positive real. Thus the pullback E={(z,V):p(V)=ρ(z)} is a locally trivial central extension of the circle by the circle. It is compact, since finitely many closed arcs inside such trivializing neighbourhoods cover the compact base and each pullback is a product with the compact fibre.
Any two lifts commute up to a scalar. Their commutator defines a continuous alternating bicharacter c(z,w) on the base: the scalar commutator is independent of phase choices and multiplicative in each argument. If z is an irrational rotation, its powers are dense and c(z,zm)=1 for every integer m. Continuity makes c(z,w)=1 for every w. Such z are themselves dense, so all the lifts commute, and E is abelian.
The tautological representation R(z,V)=V is strongly continuous. Choose a unit vector ξ and average its rank-one orthogonal projection over Haar measure on E:
K=∫E​R(e)∣ξ⟩⟨ξ∣R(e)∗de.
(22)
The integrand is trace-norm continuous, so K is positive compact with trace one, and commutes with R(E). A positive eigenvalue has a nonzero finite-dimensional eigenspace invariant under E. Commuting unitary matrices on that space have a common unit eigenvector η. Therefore R(e)η=χ(e)η for a continuous character χ of E.
On the central fibre, R(1,λI)=λI, so χ(1,λI)=λ. Consequently
Uz​=χ(z,V)−1Vfor any lift V of ρ(z)​
(23)
is independent of that lift. It is a homomorphism and strongly continuous, because the continuous map on E descends through its quotient to the base. It satisfies p(Uz​)=ρ(z). This proves circle projective representations lift to unitary representations using an actual central character, rather than assuming a global choice of phases.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
First, all lifts of the real one-parameter projective group commute. Its scalar commutator c(s,t) is again a continuous alternating bicharacter. For fixed nonzero t and an integer n>0, a lift of t is a phase multiple of the nth power of a lift of t/n; hence c(t,t/n)=1 and c(t,mt/n)=1 for every integer m. Rational multiples of t are dense in R, so continuity makes c(t,s)=1 for every s.
Choose a unitary U representing ρ(1) and the allowed self-adjoint logarithm A∈U′′ with U=eiA. Every lift of ρ(t) commutes with U, hence with A by the double commutant theorem for star-algebras condition. Therefore
ρ​(t)=ρ(t)p(e−itA)
(24)
is a continuous projective homomorphism, with ρ​(1)=1. It is periodic of period one and descends to R/Z. Part (b) lifts it to a continuous unitary homomorphism L of that circle. Each L(t) is a lift of ρ​(t) and commutes with A, since a representative has the form of an original lift times e−itA. Thus
Ut​=L(tmodZ)eitA​
(25)
is a strongly continuous unitary homomorphism with projective class ρ(t). This gives the required lift of the whole real group, not just unrelated unitary representatives at each time.

The Fredholm index measures the finite-dimensional obstruction to inverting an operator. For a bounded operator T:H1​→H2​ between Hilbert spaces, the Fredholm conditions are that its range of a bounded linear operator is closed and its kernel and cokernel are finite-dimensional. The orthogonal complement of the range is kerT∗, so
indT=dimkerT−dimkerT∗.​
(26)
An invertible linear map has Fredholm index zero; the converse needs an additional finite-dimensional correction, since an operator can have equally large kernel and cokernel.
First construct an inverse up to finite-rank operators. On (kerT)⊥, the restriction of T is a bounded bijection onto its closed range, with bounded inverse by the bounded inverse theorem. Extend that inverse by zero on (ranT)⊥, obtaining S:H2​→H1​. Then
ST=I−PkerT​,TS=I−PkerT∗​.
(27)
Conversely, suppose ST−I and TS−I are compact operators. On kerT, the first identity expresses the identity as a compact operator, so this kernel is finite-dimensional. If T were not bounded below on (kerT)⊥, there would be unit vectors xj​ in that complement with Txj​→0. Write ST=I+K. Compactness of K gives a subsequence for which Kxj​ converges, hence xj​=STxj​−Kxj​ converges to a unit vector x in (kerT)⊥ with Tx=0, a contradiction. This lower bound makes the range closed. Applying the analogous argument to T∗, using S∗T∗=I+K′∗, proves that its kernel is finite-dimensional. This proves the Atkinson theorem: a bounded operator is Fredholm exactly when it has an inverse modulo compact operators. For operators on one Hilbert space this says that its image in the Calkin algebra is invertible.
The Fredholm index is stable. Decompose the domain as N⊕N⊥, where N=kerT, and the target as C⊕R, where C=kerT∗ and R=ranT. A sufficiently small norm perturbation has block matrix
T+E=(ac​bD​),D:N⊥⟶R invertible.
(28)
Multiplying by invertible triangular block matrices reduces this matrix to the direct sum of D and the Schur complement a−bD−1c:N→C. The latter's kernel dimension minus cokernel dimension is dimN−dimC, whatever its rank. Therefore the Fredholm set is open and the index is locally constant. If K is compact, the same parametrix works modulo compact operators for every T+tK, 0≤t≤1. Local constancy along this path gives
ind(T+K)=indT.
(29)
For Fredholm operators A:H1​→H2​ and B:H2​→H3​, multiplication of parametrices shows that BA is Fredholm. Its index is additive. Here is a direct proof, rather than an assertion of additivity. There is an exact sequence of finite-dimensional spaces
0⟶kerA⟶kerBAA​kerB⟶cokerAB​cokerBA⟶cokerB⟶0.
(30)
The map from kerB takes a vector to its class modulo ranA; the next takes the class of y to that of By; the last is the quotient map. For example, a class y+ranA lies in the kernel of the middle map exactly when By=BAx for some x, so y−Ax∈kerB. This verifies the only less immediate exactness assertion; the others follow directly from their definitions. Alternating the dimensions gives
ind(BA)=indB+indA.
(31)
Also indT∗=−indT, and indices add under direct sums. For I+K with K compact, the index is zero, so injectivity is equivalent to surjectivity. More generally Tx=f is solvable exactly when f is orthogonal to kerT∗: these are the finitely many compatibility conditions in the Fredholm alternative.
Toeplitz operators exhibit how this analytic index detects a topological winding. Let H2⊂L2(S1) be the Hardy space of the circle, spanned by 1,z,z2,…, and let P be its orthogonal projection. For a continuous symbol g, define Tg​=PMg​∣H2​, where Mg​ is multiplication by g. Then ∥Tg​∥≤∥g∥∞​. The product defect is
Tf​Tg​−Tfg​=−PMf​(I−P)Mg​∣H2​.
(32)
For trigonometric polynomials the crossing of negative and nonnegative Fourier modes has finite rank. Uniform approximation of continuous symbols by trigonometric polynomials, together with the displayed norm estimate, therefore makes this defect a compact operator for all continuous f,g. If g is nowhere zero, 1/g is continuous and T1/g​ is a two-sided parametrix modulo compact operators. Thus Tg​ is Fredholm.
The converse is instructive. If g(ζ)=0 at ζ∈S1, consider the normalized Hardy kernels
kr,ζ​(z)=1−rζ​z1−r2​​,0<r<1.
(33)
Their norms are one, their individual Fourier coefficients tend to zero as r↑1, and hence they converge weakly to zero. Their squared moduli are the Poisson kernel, so continuity of g gives
∥Tg​kr,ζ​∥22​≤∥gkr,ζ​∥22​=∫S1​∣g(z)∣2∣kr,ζ​(z)∣22π∣dz∣​⟶0.
(34)
A Fredholm operator is bounded below off its finite-dimensional kernel. The projection of these weakly vanishing vectors onto that kernel tends to zero, contradicting this lower bound. Thus a continuous-symbol Toeplitz operator is Fredholm exactly when its symbol never vanishes. Applying the same argument to g−λ gives its essential spectrum as g(S1), with essential spectrum defined by failure of the Fredholm property.
For nonvanishing g, let m=wind(g,0). Lifting a continuous argument of g(eit) on 0≤t≤2π gives an argument change 2πm. After division by zm, its argument has matching endpoints, so there is a continuous function h:S1→C with g(z)=zmeh(z). The nonvanishing-symbol homotopy gt​=zmeth reduces the index to that of Tzm​. For m≥0 this is the mth power of the unilateral shift operator, whose kernel is zero and whose range has codimension m. For m<0 it is the (−m)th power of the adjoint shift, whose kernel has dimension −m and whose range is all of H2. Consequently
indTg​=−wind(g,0).​
(35)
The minus sign comes from counting missing nonnegative Fourier modes. This is a concrete bridge between the Fredholm index, stability under compact perturbations, and the winding number of a loop.

On the torus Tn=(R/2πZ)n, choose normalized Haar measure, so that ek​(x)=eik⋅x, k∈Zn, is an orthonormal basis of L2. A periodic Sobolev space is defined, for any real s, by
Hs(Tn)={u:∑k∈Zn​(1+∣k∣2)s∣u(k)∣2<∞},∥u∥Hs2​=∑k​(1+∣k∣2)s∣u(k)∣2.
(36)
For negative s, the coefficients describe distributions rather than necessarily functions. For a nonnegative integer s, the weight is comparable to ∑∣α∣≤s​∣kα∣2, so this norm is equivalent to the sum of the squared L2 norms of all weak derivatives through order s. Fourier truncation proves that smooth trigonometric polynomials are dense. The L2 pairing identifies the continuous dual of Hs with H−s, giving Sobolev duality.
Two Fourier estimates explain the usefulness of these spaces. If s>m+n/2, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
∑k​∣k∣m∣u(k)∣≤∥u∥Hs​(∑k​(1+∣k∣2)s∣k∣2m​)1/2<∞.
(37)
Uniform convergence of the differentiated Fourier series proves the Sobolev embedding Hs↪Cm. If δ>0, a bounded subset of Hs+δ has uniformly small high-frequency tails in Hs:
∑∣k∣>R​(1+∣k∣2)s∣u(k)∣2≤(1+R2)−δ∥u∥Hs+δ2​.
(38)
Finite-dimensional Fourier truncation therefore proves the compact embedding Hs+δ↪Hs, the periodic version of Rellich-Kondrachov compactness theorem. In addition, for s>n/2 multiplication is continuous Hs×Hs→Hs, making it a Sobolev algebra. Indeed the weighted coefficient of a product is bounded by the sum of the convolutions of ⟨k⟩s∣u(k)∣ with ∣v(k)∣ and of ∣u(k)∣ with ⟨k⟩s∣v(k)∣; Cauchy-Schwarz puts unweighted coefficients in ℓ1, and the ℓ1∗ℓ2→ℓ2 case of Young's convolution inequality finishes the estimate.
For eigenfunction expansions, distinguish ellipticity from self-adjointness. An arbitrary non-self-adjoint elliptic operator need not have an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions. A useful definite setting is
Lu=−∑i,j​∂i​(aij​(x)∂j​u)+V(x)u,
(39)
with smooth real periodic coefficients, aij​=aji​, real V, and uniform ellipticity
∑i,j​aij​(x)ξi​ξj​≥c∣ξ∣2(c>0).
(40)
Take the self-adjoint realization in L2 with domain H2. Its construction and spectral properties can be seen from the associated form on H1,
b(u,v)=∫(∑i,j​aij​∂j​u∂i​v​+Vuv).
(41)
For a sufficiently large constant C, bC​=b+C(⋅,⋅) is a positive coercive form: bC​(u,u)≥c1​∥u∥H12​, and L+C≥I. The Lax-Milgram theorem supplies the unique weak solution of (L+C)u=f for f∈H−1; the form is Hermitian, which gives symmetry of its inverse on L2.
The regularity input is the periodic elliptic estimate
∥u∥Hs+2​≤Cs​(∥Lu∥Hs​+∥u∥Hs​).
(42)
Here is why an elliptic operator gains two derivatives. With coefficients frozen at a point, its principal symbol ∑aij​ξi​ξj​ dominates c∣ξ∣2, and the estimate follows by multiplying Fourier coefficients by that symbol. On a sufficiently small coordinate patch, the difference of the leading coefficients from these constants has arbitrarily small supremum norm. In the integer-order differentiated estimate, this absorbs the highest derivatives into the left side; derivatives falling on coefficients contribute only lower-order terms. A partition of unity reduces the variable-coefficient problem to such patches. Its commutators with L have order one, controlled by
∥u∥Hs+1​≤ε∥u∥Hs+2​+Cε​∥u∥Hs​,
(43)
which follows by splitting low and high Fourier modes. Absorbing these terms gives the displayed estimate. For a weak H1 solution, the same localization with difference quotients first bounds its second weak derivatives for f∈L2; differentiating and repeating then gives f∈Hs⇒u∈Hs+2 for nonnegative integer s. Interpolation and duality extend the scale to real orders. In particular (L+C)−1:L2→H2 is bounded.
Let R=(L+C)−1. Compactness of H2↪L2 makes R a compact operator. Symmetry of the form makes R self-adjoint, and positivity of L+C makes R positive and injective. Its range is dense because kerR∗=kerR=0. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators consequently gives an orthonormal basis ϕj​ with
Rϕj​=μj​ϕj​,μj​>0,μj​⟶0,Lϕj​=λj​ϕj​,λj​=μj−1​−C⟶+∞.
(44)
Elliptic regularity bootstraps every ϕj​ to a smooth function. Each eigenvalue has finite multiplicity. Thus a self-adjoint uniformly elliptic second-order operator on the torus has a complete smooth orthonormal eigenfunction expansion with discrete eigenvalues tending to infinity.
Writing uj​=(u,ϕj​), every u∈L2 has u=∑j​uj​ϕj​ in L2, with ∥u∥22​=∑j​∣uj​∣2. Iterating the elliptic estimate shows that the graph norm of (L+C)m is equivalent to the H2m norm. Interpolation and duality give the more general spectral description
∥u∥Hs2​≍j∑​(λj​+C)s∣uj​∣2.​
(45)
The comparison constants depend on the operator and s. In particular smooth functions have coefficients decaying faster than every power of λj​+C, and their expansions converge in every Sobolev norm and hence in every Cm norm.
This gives a practical way to solve elliptic equations. The equation Lu=f is solvable if and only if fj​=0 whenever λj​=0; then one may take uj​=fj​/λj​ on the other eigenspaces and add an arbitrary vector in kerL. The Sobolev description proves the two-derivative gain and the Fredholm alternative, rather than leaving them as formal series manipulations. Similarly the solution of the heat equation ∂t​u+Lu=0 is
u(t)=∑j​e−tλj​uj​(0)ϕj​.
(46)
For every t>0 the exponential decay at high eigenvalues places this solution in every Sobolev space, hence it is smooth.
For the Laplacian −Δ the eigenfunctions are precisely eik⋅x with eigenvalues ∣k∣2. The number with ∣k∣2≤R is the number of lattice points in a radius-R​ ball, asymptotic to its volume by comparison with unit cubes. For the general self-adjoint operator above, bounds on its form above and below by positive multiples of ∥∇u∥22​ plus constants, together with the Courant–Fischer min-max principle, imply λj​+C≍j2/n. Thus the growth reflects dimension and the two-derivative order. Compactness of the torus is essential: on Rn, translated bumps prevent the compact embedding, and the Laplacian instead has continuous spectrum described by the Fourier transform.

Use the unitary normalization of the Fourier transform,
Ff(ξ)=(2π)−n/2∫Rn​e−ix⋅ξf(x)dx,Gg(x)=(2π)−n/2∫Rn​eix⋅ξg(ξ)dξ.
(47)
The Schwartz space S(Rn) consists of smooth functions for which every Schwartz seminorm supx​∣xα∂βf(x)∣ is finite. Such functions and all their derivatives are integrable. Differentiating under the integral and integrating by parts give
∂ξα​Ff=(−i)∣α∣F(xαf),ξβFf=(−i)∣β∣F(∂βf).
(48)
Consequently
supξ​∣ξβ∂ξα​Ff(ξ)∣≤(2π)−n/2∥∂β(xαf)∥1​.
(49)
Expand the derivative by the product rule and insert the integrable weight (1+∣x∣)−n−1; the right side is bounded by finitely many Schwartz seminorms of f. This proves continuity F:S→S. The identical argument with the opposite sign proves continuity of G.
For surjectivity and injectivity an inversion proof is needed. If f∈S, multiply Ff(ξ) by e−ε∣ξ∣2/2. Fubini's theorem and the elementary Gaussian integral give
G(e−ε∣ξ∣2/2Ff)(x)=∫Rn​f(y)ρε​(x−y)dy,ρε​(x)=(2πε)−n/2e−∣x∣2/(2ε).
(50)
The Gaussian has total integral one and its mass outside any fixed ball tends to zero. The right side therefore tends to f(x), by uniform continuity of f. On the left, Ff∈S⊂L1, so dominated convergence gives GFf(x). This proves GF=I. Reversing the signs in the same calculation proves FG=I. Thus
F:S(Rn)⟶S(Rn) is a continuous bijection, with inverse G.​
(51)
Its inverse is continuous by the seminorm estimate already proved. This establishes the requested bijection without assuming Fourier inversion as an unexplained theorem.
Inversion gives F2f(x)=f(−x) and the Parseval identity. Indeed, inserting the integral for Ff into ∫FfFg​ and using f,Fg∈L1 gives ∫fg​. Density of Schwartz functions in L2 extends F to a unitary operator on L2, the Plancherel theorem. Translation of f becomes multiplication by a phase, modulation becomes frequency translation, and
F(f∗g)=(2π)n/2(Ff)(Fg),F(∂j​f)=iξj​Ff.
(52)
These formulas explain why the Fourier transform diagonalizes constant-coefficient differential operators. By transpose it also defines a bijection of the tempered distributions: with the complex-linear distributional pairing, ⟨FT,ϕ⟩=⟨T,Fϕ⟩, since the Fourier kernel is symmetric in its variables.
The connection with creation and annihilation operators is especially transparent for the harmonic oscillator. On the common invariant dense domain S, set
aj​=2​xj​+∂j​​,aj†​=2​xj​−∂j​​.
(53)
Integration by parts shows that these are formal Hilbert-space adjoints. They are closable unbounded operators; commutators below are computed on S, avoiding undefined products on arbitrary L2 vectors. The identity [∂j​,xk​]=δjk​I gives the canonical commutation relations
[aj​,ak†​]=δjk​I,[aj​,ak​]=[aj†​,ak†​]=0.
(54)
It also gives
H=−Δ+∣x∣2=2∑j​aj†​aj​+nI.
(55)
The normalized vacuum h0​(x)=π−n/4e−∣x∣2/2 satisfies aj​h0​=0. Define the Hermite functions
hα​=α1​!⋯αn​!​(a1†​)α1​⋯(an†​)αn​​h0​.
(56)
Moving annihilation operators past creation operators with the commutation relations proves
aj​hα​=αj​​hα−ej​​,aj†​hα​=αj​+1​hα+ej​​,Hhα​=(2∣α∣+n)hα​.
(57)
These same relations show that the Hermite functions are orthonormal: unequal occupations are orthogonal eigenvectors of one of the commuting symmetric number operators aj†​aj​, and the ladder relations recursively give norm one.
For completeness, let g∈L2 be orthogonal to every hα​. The Hermite polynomials have nonzero leading monomials and triangular lower-degree terms, so these orthogonality relations say that all polynomial moments of h(x)=g(x)e−∣x∣2/2∈L1 vanish. Its Fourier integral extends to an entire function of ζ∈Cn:
F(ζ)=∫g(x)e−∣x∣2/2e−ix⋅ζdx.
(58)
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, with the Gaussian absorbing every exponential linear weight and every polynomial, justifies differentiation uniformly on compact sets of ζ. Every Taylor coefficient at zero is a vanishing moment, so the entire function is zero. Fourier uniqueness on L1 follows here without circularity: if an L1 function has zero Fourier transform, convolving it with ρε​ gives zero by the Gaussian integral and Fubini, and the approximate-identity limit in L1 gives the original function zero. Thus h=0 and g=0. The Hermite functions form an orthonormal basis of L2.
Finally, the elementary Gaussian integral gives Fh0​=h0​. The derivative and multiplication identities above imply
Faj​=iaj​F,Faj†​=−iaj†​F,
(59)
where the operators on the right act on the frequency variable. Hence
Fhα​=(−i)∣α∣hα​.​
(60)
Thus creation and annihilation organize both the oscillator's spectral decomposition and the four possible Fourier eigenvalues. On Schwartz functions the oscillator powers control weighted derivatives, and Hermite coefficients decay faster than every power of 1+∣α∣; conversely this rapid coefficient decay implies all Schwartz seminorms are finite. The Fourier phases preserve this decay, providing another explanation of the Fourier automorphism of Schwartz space.

The loop group here is LU(1)=C∞(S1,U(1)), with pointwise multiplication. Although it is abelian, its nontrivial positive-energy quantum representations are projective: implementers can commute only up to a phase. A positive energy representation of the loop group of U(1) has rotations Rt​ whose self-adjoint generator is bounded below and which implement g(z)↦g(eitz) in the projective unitary group. The fermionic construction gives both that phase and an explicit bosonic description.
Choose the one-particle Hilbert space H=L2(S1) with modes er​(z)=zr, r∈Z, and projection P onto r≥0. Use the polarized fermionic Fock space
FP​=Λ(PH)⊗​Λ((I−P)H​),
(61)
where the exterior powers are Hilbert-completed and the tensor product is graded. Its vacuum fills all modes r<0 and leaves r≥0 empty; excitations are particles in the empty modes and holes in the filled modes. The fermionic annihilation operators cr​ and fermionic creation operators cr∗​ satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations
{cr​,cs∗​}=δrs​I,{cr​,cs​}={cr∗​,cs∗​}=0,cr​Ω=0 (r≥0),cr∗​Ω=0 (r<0).
(62)
Finite particle-hole configurations form an orthonormal basis. As in the finite-dimensional exterior algebra construction, their creation and annihilation operators act irreducibly: an operator in the commutant sends the vacuum to a scalar vacuum, since the joint kernel of its vacuum annihilators is one-dimensional, and then acts by that scalar on the dense configuration basis.
Segal's quantization criterion for fermions says that a unitary one-particle operator u has a unitary implementer Γ(u) on this Fock space, satisfying Γ(u)c∗(f)Γ(u)∗=c∗(uf), exactly when
[P,u] is Hilbert-Schmidt.​
(63)
Equivalently P−uPu∗ is Hilbert-Schmidt. Implementers are unique up to phase, hence form a projective unitary representation of the restricted unitary group. This is the fermionic, polarized criterion; it is not a condition that the entire operator u−I be Hilbert-Schmidt. The criterion and the corresponding continuity topology are stated in Theorem III.2.1.1 of the fermionic construction of loop-group representations. For the compact principal-angle part of a pair of polarizations, the threshold has a concrete interpretation. Its two-dimensional blocks are rotations through angles θj​; finitely many unmatched modes can be handled separately. Each angle θj​ rotates the vacuum into cosθj​ times its original component plus sinθj​ times a particle-hole pair. After discarding finitely many exceptional blocks, the successive tensor products are Cauchy precisely when ∏j​cosθj​ converges to a nonzero value, equivalently ∑j​sin2θj​<∞. In this block model the sum is exactly half the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the projection difference; finitely many unmatched modes account for a change of charge. Infinitely many unmatched modes already violate the criterion. This explains why infinitely many arbitrarily small mixings can fail to be implementable.
For g(z)=∑n​gn​zn∈LU(1), multiplication Mg​ is a unitary one-particle operator. Its matrix entry from es​ to er​ is gr−s​. Therefore
∥[P,Mg​]∥HS2​=∑r,s​∣1r≥0​−1s≥0​∣2∣gr−s​∣2=∑n∈Z​∣n∣∣gn​∣2.
(64)
For a fixed difference n, exactly ∣n∣ pairs cross the polarization boundary. Smoothness makes the sum finite, so Segal's quantization criterion for fermions constructs a continuous projective unitary representation of every smooth loop. Smooth convergence gives operator-norm convergence of Mg​ and Hilbert-Schmidt convergence of its commutator, which is sufficient for the strong projective continuity of the implementers.
Normal ordering fixes the charge and rotation energy. On the dense finite-configuration domain put
Ers​=:cr∗​cs​:=cr∗​cs​−δrs​1r<0​I,Q=∑r​Err​,L0​=∑r​rErr​.
(65)
The sums are finite on each configuration. A particle at r≥0 adds charge one and energy r; a hole at r<0 adds charge minus one and energy −r. Consequently L0​ is a nonnegative self-adjoint diagonal operator with integer spectrum and finite-dimensional eigenspaces. The unitaries Rt​=eitL0​ are strongly continuous, have period 2π, and implement er​↦eitrer​. Conjugating multiplication by this one-particle rotation gives Mg(eit⋅)​, so their Fock implementers rotate the loop representation projectively. This is an actual positive-energy circle action.
The scalar anomaly is visible in the Heisenberg current algebra of a fermion on the circle. Define on finite-energy vectors
Jn​=∑r∈Z​Er,r+n​,Jn∗​=J−n​,J0​=Q.
(66)
For fixed n the sum has only finitely many nonzero actions on any configuration. Direct use of the canonical anticommutation relations gives
[Ers​,Etu​]=δst​Eru​−δur​Ets​+δst​δur​(1r<0​−1s<0​)I.
(67)
On summing, the two noncentral sums cancel. If m=−n the central sum is ∑r​(1r<0​−1r+n<0​)=n: for n>0 the terms are precisely r=−n,…,−1. Thus
[Jn​,Jm​]=nδn+m,0​I,[L0​,Jn​]=−nJn​.​
(68)
In particular Jn​Ω=0 for n>0. The coefficient one in the central term is the level of this basic representation.
Let h(θ)=∑n​hn​einθ be smooth and real. The normal-ordered infinitesimal implementer of multiplication by h is
A(h)=∑n​hn​J−n​.
(69)
The sign of the current index matters: multiplication by zn raises the one-particle mode by n, so it corresponds to J−n​. It follows either directly from the bilinear commutator or from the fermionic currents on the circle that [A(h),cr∗​]=∑n​hn​cr+n∗​. For trigonometric h these are oscillator fields on the finite-energy domain; their self-adjoint closures exponentiate to the implementers of eih. For general smooth h, their extensions are obtained by the oscillator-field construction below: ∑n>0​n∣hn​∣2<∞ guarantees the square-summable field coefficients, and Fourier truncation converges in the corresponding Weyl relations implementers. Thus no unjustified infinite operator product is required.
Set
ω(h,k)=2π1​∫02π​h′(θ)k(θ)dθ=i∑n​nhn​k−n​.
(70)
It is real and antisymmetric for real h,k. The Heisenberg current algebra of a fermion on the circle relations give [A(h),A(k)]=iω(h,k)I. The Weyl relations, or the finite-mode Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff computation followed by the square-summable limit, yield
eiA(h)eiA(k)=e−iω(h,k)/2eiA(h+k).
(71)
This is an explicit two-cocycle on the identity component of the loop group. A different phase choice changes it by a group coboundary, but its antisymmetric commutator remains e−iω(h,k), and hence cannot be removed.
The winding components also matter. Every smooth loop is zweih with w∈Z, real periodic h, and mean h0​ determined modulo 2π. Let S implement multiplication by z. It moves the filled boundary one place upwards, so it raises charge by one; phases of charge ground states can be chosen so that SΩq​=Ωq+1​. Conjugating the fermionic currents on the circle gives
SQS∗=Q−I,SJn​S∗=Jn​(n=0).
(72)
Choose U(w,h)=SweiA(h). Since eiA(h)Sv=Svei(A(h)+vh0​I), one obtains the full loop group two-cocycle for U(1)
U(w,h)U(v,k)=c((w,h),(v,k))U(w+v,h+k),c((w,h),(v,k))=exp(ivh0​−iω(h,k)/2).​
(73)
The exponent is bilinear in the additive winding-logarithm coordinates, so expansion immediately gives c(a,b)c(a+b,d)=c(b,d)c(a,b+d). Replacing h by h+2πℓ changes A(h) by 2πℓQ, whose exponential is identity since charges are integers; the scalar cocycle also stays unchanged since v∈Z. Thus the expression is well-defined on loops, not just on chosen logarithms. It records both the derivative anomaly and the commutator of winding with constant loops.
For the fermion-boson correspondence on the circle, decompose FP​=⨁q∈Z​Fq​ into charge eigenspaces. The charge-q ground state Ωq​ fills all integer modes r<q. Its energy is
L0​Ωq​=2q(q−1)​Ωq​.
(74)
For q>0, sum the energies of the added modes 0,…,q−1; for q<0, sum the hole energies of the removed modes q,…,−1. Every other charge-q configuration is obtained by moving finitely many occupied levels upwards, so this is the lowest energy. Since Jn​ preserves charge and lowers energy by n>0, Jn​Ωq​=0 for n>0.
Define bosonic annihilation operators bn​=Jn​/n​ and bn∗​=J−n​/n​, n>0. They obey [bn​,bm∗​]=δnm​I. Their occupation vectors
∏n>0​nmn​mn​!​(J−n​)mn​​Ωq​,mn​∈N0​ with finite support,
(75)
are orthonormal by commuting positive fermionic currents on the circle through negative fermionic currents on the circle. Their energies are q(q−1)/2+∑n>0​nmn​. It remains to prove that they span, rather than assume the boson correspondence. Count configurations by formal charge u and energy t. Empty modes r≥0 can contain one extra particle, while filled modes −r, r≥1, can contain one hole. Therefore the fermionic character is
∏r≥0​(1+utr)∏r≥1​(1+u−1tr).
(76)
The charge form of the Jacobi triple product proved in Question 4 identifies this with
∑q∈Z​∏n≥1​(1−tn)uqtq(q−1)/2​.
(77)
The reciprocal product counts bosonic occupations, or partitions of an integer. For fixed charge and energy, the finite-dimensional fermion space has exactly as many basis configurations as the independent fermionic current on the circle monomials already constructed. Hence those monomials exhaust every such space, proving their dense completeness. This establishes a unitary identification of every charge sector with a bosonic Fock space, and on that identification
L0​=2Q(Q−I)​+n>0∑​nbn∗​bn​.​
(78)
The usual half-integer fermion convention instead gives ground energy q2/2 and requires the corresponding adjustment of rotations. Here integer modes were deliberately chosen to obtain a genuine circle action with integral nonnegative energies. The two ground states of energy zero, at charges zero and one, are therefore consistent, not a negative-energy defect.
This is also a constructive bosonic realization of the loop representation: the mean of h acts by h0​Q, nonzero modes of h act as the square-summable oscillator field ∑n>0​n​(hn​bn∗​+hn​​bn​), and winding shifts the charge sectors. Taking k tensor copies adds the fermionic current on the circle central terms and gives level k∈N. Positivity constrains their sign, since in a vacuum sector ∥J−n​Ω∥2=kn for n>0. The level-one construction, its explicit loop cocycle, and its complete bosonic occupation basis show how an abelian classical loop group acquires noncommuting quantum currents while retaining positive rotation energy.
